A low agreement rate is a measure of policy difference, not of error in either policy.

finding: Workload concentration is far worse under the recommended policy, and this is the clearest consequence of the static counterfactual
evidence: The busiest decile of RMs receives 72.31% of recommendations against 33.99% historically; Gini 0.773 against 0.458. One RM receives 3,234 recommendations where the historical maximum is 663, and 8 of 140 RMs receive none at all. This is driven by the static counterfactual: a recommendation never consumes capacity, so the same lightly loaded RM keeps winning RPF-05 and RPF-06 at every decision in its territory. What the distribution would look like under a live capacity ledger that each recommendation decrements is untested here, and any operational use would need one. Nothing in this evidence supports a claim that the declared rules balance workload better than the historical policy; on this evidence they concentrate it.

finding: Channel self-assignment and the named preferred RM are not modelled
evidence: RT-E05 lets an RM-prospected lead self-assign to the prospecting RM, and RT-P05 honours a referrer's named preferred RM. Neither rule is implemented here, because neither input is available as an as-of field on the synthetic lead. Agreement with the historical policy by channel is CH-PTR 23.71%, CH-BRN 24.71%, CH-DIG 24.93%, CH-MKT 25.25%, CH-RMP 30.93%. The spread is narrow, so the missing rules do not explain the overall difference between the two policies; the preference ranking does.
